findings.title: Denial cache reintroduces the exact bug this PR is meant to fix
findings.body: The new negative cache caches a deny decision for shortCacheTTL (30s) keyed on (namespace, user, action, resource name, parent folder), and there is no invalidation when permissions or resources change. Scenario: a user requests a dashboard that does not yet exist / they have no permission for (Check returns deny and the entry is written at line 154). The user then creates that dashboard or folder (or an admin grants access). The very next Check for the same resource hits the denial entry at line 117 and is denied for up to 30 seconds, with no DB fallback. This is precisely the 'creator can't access the dashboard they just created' failure the PR description says it fixes — it is now bounded to ~30s instead of removed. Same for newly granted permissions: access is delayed by up to 30s. Consider invalidating the denial entry on writes, keying it more coarsely with shorter TTL, or not caching denials when the resource was simply absent from the scope map.

findings.title: Denial cache key can collide with permission cache key (unescaped underscore concatenation)
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by plain underscore concatenation: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Both userUID and name/parent are attacker-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores, so two distinct (user, action, name, parent) tuples can produce the same key (e.g. uid "a", action "x", name "b_c" vs uid "a", action "x", name "b", parent "c" with an underscore shift). Worse, the key shares the "<ns>.perm_" prefix space with userPermCacheKey(ns, userUID, action), so a denial entry for one user/action tuple can be read as another user's permission set (or vice versa) if components line up — in Check, permCache.Get is keyed by the same scheme and the denial cache shares the same underlying cache.Cache instance. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions (or hash/encode components) to make the keys unambiguous.

findings.title: No test that a deny decision actually writes the denial cache entry
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' case only verifies that a manually pre-populated permDenialCache entry causes a deny. There is no test asserting that after Check returns Allowed=false from a DB query, the service writes the denial entry (service.go:154) and that a subsequent Check for the same resource short-circuits without hitting the store. This is the core new behavior of the PR (negative caching) and its write path is untested; a regression that never writes the entry (making the whole feature a no-op) would pass the current suite.

findings.title: Denial-cache hit misreported as a permission-cache hit in permissionCacheUsage metric
findings.body: When the denial cache is hit, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit) even though the permission cache was not consulted. Additionally, when cached permissions exist but evaluate to deny, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" (line 137) despite the perm cache actually being hit. Both skew the cache-hit-rate metric in opposite directions, making it unusable for evaluating whether the caching changes are effective.

findings.title: Deny path with cached permissions always re-queries the DB, defeating singleflight in common case
findings.body: When a user has cached permissions that don't cover the requested resource (a very common deny case for legitimate users, e.g. dashboard they don't own), Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and performs a full DB permission query, and a denial entry is only written afterward. For users with genuinely no permission for the action at all, getIdentityPermissions returns an empty/stale-cached scope map which is re-fetched and re-set into permCache each time before checkPermission denies. The permCache is refreshed with identical data on every request for such users (singleflight only dedups concurrent, not sequential calls). Consider not re-setting permCache when the fetched map is identical, or caching 'no permissions for action' explicitly, to avoid write amplification on the hot deny path.
